learning_objective: 🎯 Cross linguistic borders! Understand the basics of translation, its importance in a multilingual world, and the difference between literal and free translation.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Translation is the process of transferring the meaning of a text from one language (the Source Language) into another language (the Target Language) while maintaining the original tone and intent.
The Source Language (SL) is the original language the text is written in. The Target Language (TL) is the language you are translating into. A good translator must be fluent in both!

This is replacing each word in the SL with its exact dictionary equivalent in the TL. It often sounds robotic, grammatically incorrect, and completely misses the cultural meaning (like Google Translate at its worst).

This focuses on translating the *meaning* rather than the exact words. The translator adapts the sentence structure and idioms so that it sounds completely natural to a native speaker of the Target Language.
A translator is a cultural bridge. They don't just translate words; they translate culture, humor, and emotions, ensuring the new audience feels exactly what the original audience felt.

fun_activity.title: 😂 The Literal Idiom Trap
fun_activity.instructions: Take the English idiom 'It's raining cats and dogs'. Translate it word-for-word literally into your mother tongue. Does it make any sense to someone who doesn't speak English? Now, write down the *actual* equivalent idiom used in your language for heavy rain!

exam_tips: 📌 Always clearly define SL (Source Language) and TL (Target Language) when answering theoretical questions on translation.
📌 A frequent exam question asks for the difference between translation and interpretation. Translation is for WRITTEN text; interpretation is for SPOKEN language.
📌 Never advocate for purely literal translation in literature. Sense-for-sense translation is almost always superior for creative writing.
quick_recap: ⭐ Translation is essentially rewriting a text for a completely new audience.
⭐ Idioms and proverbs are the hardest things to translate because they are deeply tied to local culture.
⭐ A perfect translation reads as if it was originally written in the Target Language.
